chunks: By his saying, peace be upon him: “Ribā is only in deferred exchange.”

So Ibn ʿAbbās considered this report as proof that there is no ribā except in deferred exchange. It also indicates that the expression “innamā” conveys what we have mentioned, namely that when the Companions disagreed regarding the meeting of the two circumcised parts, those who did not regard that as making ghusl obligatory used it as evidence.

key_terms.إِنَّمَا: a particle indicating restriction or exclusivity
key_terms.الرِّبَا: usury; unlawful increase in financial exchange
key_terms.النَّسِيئَةِ: deferred exchange or delay in payment
key_terms.الْتِقَاءِ الْخِتَانَيْنِ: the meeting of the two circumcised parts, a juristic expression for sexual contact
key_terms.الْخَبَرَ: the report or hadith being cited as evidence
key_terms.الْغُسْلِ: ghusl (ritual bath), here referring to obligatory major purification

ai.seo_question: How does the phrase “innamā” indicate restriction in Shia hadith-based legal reasoning?
ai.summary: This passage cites the statement “Ribā is only in deferred exchange” and notes that Ibn ʿAbbās understood it as restricting ribā to cases of deferment. It also uses the wording “innamā” as evidence for exclusivity in legal reasoning, connecting that principle to a juristic disagreement over whether the meeting of the two circumcised parts necessitates ghusl.
